'''''Rhododendron ponticum''''', called '''common rhododendron''' or '''pontic rhododendron''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the heath family [[Ericaceae]]. It is native to the [[Iberian Peninsula]] in southwest [[Europe]] and the [[Caucasus]] region in northern [[West Asia]].
[[File:Bloeiwijze Rhododendron (Rhododendron ponticum). 19-05-2026 (d.j.b.).jpg|thumb|250px| Flower of ''Rhododendron ponticum'']]

==Description==
''R. ponticum'' is a dense, [[sucker (botany)|suckering]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] growing to {{convert|5|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, rarely {{convert|8|m|ft|abbr=on}}. The [[leaf|leaves]] are [[evergreen]], {{convert|6|to|18|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|to|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide. The [[flower]]s are {{convert|3.5|to|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, violet-purple, often with small greenish-yellow spots or streaks. The [[fruit]] is a dry [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] {{convert|1.5|to|2.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} long, containing numerous small [[seed]]s.

It has two [[subspecies]]:

==Distribution and habitat==
The species has two [[Disjunct distribution|disjunct populations]], one in the southwestern [[Iberian Peninsula]] (central and southern [[Portugal]] and southwestern [[Spain]]) and the other near the southern [[Black Sea Basin]] (eastern [[Bulgaria]], northern [[Turkey]], [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], and [[Northern Caucasus]]). It has also been introduced to [[Madeira]], [[Myanmar]], [[Belgium]], the [[British Isles]], [[Netherlands]] and [[France]].<ref name=POWO/><ref name=ponticum />

In the Iberian Peninsula, the range is limited to the montane environments of the [[Serra do Caramulo|Caramulo mountains]], the [[Serra de Monchique|Monchique range]] and the [[Los Alcornocales Natural Park|Aljibe range]]. These are remnants of the original [[laurissilva]] forests that covered the peninsula 66 million years ago.<ref name="Évora">{{cite web |title=A adelfeira de Monchique |date=13 March 2018 |url=http://www.liferelict.ect.uevora.pt/index.php/adelfeiras/ |publisher=[[University of Évora]] |access-date=21 November 2020}}</ref>

Though the common rhododendron was present in [[Great Britain]] prior to the [[Last Glacial Period|most recent ice age]], it did not recolonise afterwards, meaning that the modern ecology of the island developed without it. Its presence today in Great Britain is due to human introduction, and it can easily become established and cause problems in some situations, often smothering entire hillsides (especially in [[Snowdonia]] and western Scotland). In the British Isles, it colonises moorlands, uplands and shady woodlands (alongside escaped laurels and the native holly), as well as areas with acidic soils.<ref name=Cross>{{cite journal |title=''Rhododendron ponticum'' L. |first=JR |last=Cross |journal=Journal of Ecology |volume=63 |issue=1 |date=1975 |pages=345–364 |doi=10.2307/2258859 |jstor=2258859 |bibcode=1975JEcol..63..345C }}</ref>

===Historical range===
[[Fossil]] evidence shows it had a much wider range across most of southern and western Europe before the [[Late Glacial Maximum]], or until about 20,000 years ago.<ref name=Cross/>

The plant was noted by the botanist [[Joseph Pitton de Tournefort]] during his travels in the Near East in 1700–1702. It was named by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] to commemorate the ancient kingdom of [[Pontus (region)|Pontus]] on the southern shores of the [[Black Sea]] where it grew.  At the other end of its range, in southern Spain, Linnaeus' friend and correspondent [[Clas Alströmer]] found it growing alongside [[oleander]].{{Citation needed|date=November 2020}} It was introduced to Britain as an ornamental [[shrub]] in 1763 and was later planted to provide cover for game birds. It is now considered to be an [[invasive species]].<ref>{{cite web|first=Alice M. |last=Coats|title=Garden Shrubs and Their Histories (1964) 1992, ''s.v.'' "Rhododendron"|url=http://www.countrysideinfo.co.uk/rhododen.htm#Introduction%20to%20Britain|website=www.countrysideinfo.co.uk}}</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
[[File:Rhododendron ponticum 2.jpg|thumb|right|Closeup of ''Rhododendron ponticum'']]''Rhododendron ponticum'' subsp. ''baeticum'' is one of the most extensively cultivated rhododendrons in western and central Europe. It is used as an [[ornamental plant]] in its own right and, more frequently, as a [[rootstock]] onto which other more attractive rhododendrons are [[grafting|grafted]]. The plants were first cultivated in Britain in the 1760s, supplied by [[Loddiges|Conrad Loddiges]], and became widely distributed through the commercial nursery trade in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. The roots readily produce suckers below the graft, which can sometimes overtake the intended grafted rhododendron.

Honey produced with pollen from the flowers of this plant can be  poisonous if consumed in sufficient quantities, causing severe [[hypotension]] and [[bradycardia]] in humans. It is known as [[mad honey]] due to its toxic diterpenes ([[grayanotoxin]]s).<ref>{{cite book|last=Hayes|first=Andrew Wallace|title=Principles and methods of toxicology|publisher=CRC Press|year=2007|page=998|isbn=978-0-8493-3778-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vgHXTId8rnYC&pg=PA998}}</ref> This poisonous honey plays a significant part in the 2023 film ''[[A Haunting in Venice]]''.

The sap from a freshly cut branch can be used to treat toothache.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Erdemoglu |first1=Nurgun |last2=Akkol |first2=Esra Küpeli |last3=Yesilada |first3=Erdem |last4=Calış |first4=Ihsan |date=2008-09-02 |title=Bioassay-guided isolation of anti-inflammatory and antinociceptive principles from a folk remedy, Rhododendron ponticum L. leaves |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378874108003395 |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=119 |issue=1 |pages=172–178 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2008.06.021 |pmid=18638535 |issn=0378-8741|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Invasive species==
Suckering of the root, together with its abundant seed production, has led to it becoming an [[invasive species]] over much of western Europe and in parts of [[New Zealand]].  Rhododendron control is a key element in nature conservation in those areas.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://forests.org/archive/general/newflfau.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010728005428/http://forests.org/archive/general/newflfau.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=2001-07-28|title=New flora and fauna for old|date=2000-12-21|newspaper=The Economist|access-date=2008-12-14}}</ref>
Conservation organisations in Britain now believe ''R. ponticum'' has become "a severe problem" in the native [[Atlantic]] [[oak]]woods of the [[Scottish Highlands|west highlands]] of [[Scotland]] and in [[Wales]] and [[Ireland]], and on [[heathland]]s in southern [[England]], crowding out the native flora.<ref>{{cite web
 | title = Rhododendron: A killer of the Countryside
 | publisher = Offwell Woodland & Wildlife Trust
 | year = 2004
 | url = http://www.countrysideinfo.co.uk/rhododen.htm
 | access-date = 30 May 2010 }}
</ref>  Clearance strategies have been developed, including the flailing and cutting down of plants with follow-up [[herbicide]] spraying. Injection of herbicide into individual plants has been found to be more precise and effective.<ref>{{cite web| title =BREAKTHROUGH IN BATTLE AGAINST PROBLEM PONTICUM| publisher =[[Forestry Commission]]| date =30 July 2004| url =http://www.forestry.gov.uk/news1/196010F167115B7180256ED9004A090C| access-date =30 May 2010| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20110305175422/http://www.forestry.gov.uk/news1/196010F167115B7180256ED9004A090C| archive-date =5 March 2011}}</ref>

In [[Ireland]], particularly in the [[Killarney National Park]] it is extremely invasive and the exact date that Rhododendrons were introduced  is unknown. It has no natural predators in Ireland and is avoided by grazing animals as the stems and leaves contain toxic levels of grayanotoxins. It is  suggested that the shrub was planted in Derrycunihy wood in the 19th century or before.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Campbell |first1=Christina |last2=Kelly |first2=Daniel L. |last3=Smyth |first3=Noeleen |last4=Lockhart |first4=Neil |last5=Holyoak |first5=David T. |last6=Long |first6=David |date=2023-06-09 |title=Investigation of the Copper Requirements of the Metallophyte Liverworts Cephaloziella nicholsonii Douin and C. massalongoi (Spruce) Müll.Frib |journal=Plants |volume=12 |issue=12 |pages=2265 |doi=10.3390/plants12122265 |doi-access=free |pmid=37375890 |pmc=10300965 |bibcode=2023Plnts..12.2265C |issn=2223-7747}}</ref>

A study<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tiedeken|first1=Erin Jo|last2=Egan|first2=Paul A.|last3=Stevenson|first3=Philip C.|last4=Wright|first4=Geraldine A.|author-link4=Geraldine Wright|last5=Brown|first5=Mark J. F.|last6=Power|first6=Eileen F.|last7=Farrell|first7=Iain|last8=Matthews|first8=Sharon M.|last9=Stout|first9=Jane C.|last10=Manson|first10=Jessamyn|title=Nectar chemistry modulates the impact of an invasive plant on native pollinators|journal=Functional Ecology|date=November 2015|pages=885–893|doi=10.1111/1365-2435.12588|volume=30|issue=6|hdl=2262/74965 |url=http://gala.gre.ac.uk/id/eprint/14020/1/14020_STEVENSON_Nectar_Chemistry_Modulates_2015.pdf|doi-access=free}}</ref> in the journal ''[[Functional Ecology (journal)|Functional Ecology]]'' also showed that invasive rhododendron nectar was toxic to European honeybees (''[[Apis mellifera]]''), killing individuals within hours of consumption. It also paralyzed bees of the species ''[[Andrena carantonica]]'', a solitary mining bee. Bees became paralysed and exhibited excessive grooming or other distress behaviours after feeding on Rhododendron nectar, and ate less food than bees fed a control nectar. In contrast the buff-tailed bumblebee (''[[Bombus terrestris]]'') was not affected by the rhododendron nectar. It is important not to see Rhododendron as a problem species for honey bees as they actually avoid the flowers owing to their ability to detect the toxin nectar. The toxicity is caused by [[grayanotoxin]] 1 which is one of several highly hydroxylated diterpenoid defence chemicals produced in the leaves of ''Rhododendron'' to protect against [[herbivore]]s – e.g. the ''[[Thrips (genus)|Thrips]]'' ''Heliothrips haemorrhoidalis''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Scott-Brown, AS, Gregory, T, Farrell, IW, Stevenson PC. |title=Leaf trichomes and foliar chemistry mediate defence against glasshouse thrips; ''Heliothrips haemorrhoidalis'' (Bouché) in ''Rhododendron simsii''. |journal=Functional Plant Biology |date=2016 |volume=43 |issue=12 |pages=1170–1182 |doi=10.1071/FP16045 |pmid=32480536 |bibcode=2016FunPB..43.1170S |url=https://www.publish.csiro.au/fp/FP16045|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Some species of honey bee (''Apis mellifera'' sub spp ''caucasica'') tolerate the toxin and make so-called "[[mad honey]]".

===Identification difficulties===
Recent efforts to control the spread of ''Rhododendron ponticum'' in the United Kingdom have led to controversy, particularly at [[Taymouth Castle]] in Highland Perthshire. The accurate identification of the plant remains a topic of debate, particularly where it is interspersed amongst clumps of cherry laurel (''Prunus laurocerasus'') in areas of mixed woodland.{{citation needed|date=June 2026}} Tensions surrounding the management of these cohabiting species came to a head in early December 2022, when prominent arboriculturalists encountered strong opposition from machine operators on the estate regarding the correct identification and subsequent management of the plant.{{citation needed|date=June 2026}}  This culminated in the destruction of a large laurel thicket. While the similarities and differences between the plants remains a subject of debate, cherry laurel may indeed be viewed and treated in the same way as rhododendron in this habitat niche.<ref>Milne, R.I. and Abbott, R.J., 2000. Origin and evolution of invasive naturalized material of Rhododendron ponticum L. in the British Isles. ''Molecular Ecology'', 9(5), pp. 541–556.</ref>
